questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What the absence of labels removes
questions.learningObjective: distinguish what an unlabelled dataset can and cannot support
questions.stem: A team holds 40,000 rows of customer activity with no column naming what happened afterwards, and wants to find groups nobody has described before. What does the absence of labels actually remove?

options.text: The ability to score a group against a known outcome, since there is no outcome column to score it against
The ability to find structure, because structure can only be recognised when a correct answer exists
options.misconception: believes structure is only real when a labelled answer confirms it

options.text: The ability to judge whether a grouping is good, because every grouping needs a labelled score
options.misconception: assumes an unlabelled grouping cannot be assessed at all

options.text: Nothing whatsoever, since the rows and the columns are the same whether or not a target is present
options.misconception: reads a missing target column as leaving the dataset unchanged

questions.explanation: Distance, density and variance are computable from the columns that exist, so grouping an unlabelled table is straightforward; what does not exist is any column to check the groups against, which is why an unlabelled result can be described but not validated. That is the whole difference between an exploratory grouping and a scored one, and it is why a later labelled result is the only way to find out whether the groups meant anything. The tempting move is to treat a visually tidy picture as though it were a validated result, but tidiness is a property of the geometry, not evidence about the outcome.
questions.hint: Ask which column a group would be scored against, and whether that column is present.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a clustering objective minimises
questions.learningObjective: name the quantity a clustering objective makes small
questions.stem: Every clustering objective is a number computed from the data, and the algorithm descends it at each step. What is being made small when a k-means objective is made small?

options.text: The spread of the points around the centre of their own group, summed over the groups
The distance from each point to the nearest point of a different group, summed over points
options.misconception: confuses within-group spread with between-group separation

options.text: The number of groups, since fewer groups always cost less to describe and to store
options.misconception: believes a lower objective is always a better-described answer

options.text: The distance between the group centres, since widely separated centres mark the better fit
options.misconception: treats centre separation as evidence that the points fit well

questions.explanation: The k-means objective is the sum, over groups, of the squared distance from each point to the centre of its own group, so a step that reduces it has pulled every point closer to the centre of the group it now sits in. Separation between centres appears nowhere in that sum, which is why a grouping can score well while its centres sit on top of each other, and why a scheme that punished centres for being close would be optimising a different quantity. The trap is natural because the picture of tidy separated groups is what we mean by a good clustering, but the objective only measures tightness.
questions.hint: Write the sum the algorithm writes down and ask what each term refers to.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A lower objective from a different starting point
questions.learningObjective: explain what a lower objective value proves about the search
questions.stem: Two runs of the same algorithm on the same data, with the same k and different starting points, end in different groupings, and the second run finishes with the lower objective value. What has the second run established?

options.text: The objective has a local floor that starting points can fall into, so finishing lower still does not mean finishing best
The data contains two groupings of equal merit, so choosing between them is a matter of taste
options.misconception: reads a strict improvement as if both answers were equally good

options.text: The algorithm is unstable and will give a different answer again on a third run of the same data
options.misconception: assumes a strict improvement implies the run has no fixed point at all

options.text: The first run computed the objective wrongly, since identical data cannot produce two different values
options.misconception: blames the arithmetic instead of the search

questions.explanation: Each run descends from wherever its starting centres happened to land, and the descent stops at a point where no single reassignment would improve the sum, which need not be the lowest such point in the whole space. A second, better stopping point therefore proves only that the first was a local one, and the standard response is to restart from several different initialisations and keep the lowest result, which is cheap and usually enough. What the comparison does not license is the belief that the winner is provably best, since proving that needs an argument the descent never makes.
questions.hint: Ask what a strict improvement rules out and what it leaves open.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The assignment step in k-means
questions.learningObjective: compute the squared distance used by the assignment step
questions.stem: Two centroids sit at (1,1) and (6,6) and a new point arrives at (3,5). The assignment step sends the point to whichever centroid is nearer. To how many squared units of distance is the point separated from the centroid it is assigned to?
questions.explanation: Squared distance to (1,1) is 4 + 16 = 20, and squared distance to (6,6) is 9 + 1 = 10, so the assignment step sends the point to (6,6) and the answer is 10. The same two numbers show where the usual slips come from: reporting 20 means the nearer centroid was picked wrongly, taking the ordinary distance rather than the squared one gives 3.16 because the objective is a sum of squares, and adding the two totals to get 30 describes a point held between the centres rather than assigned to either. Every one of those is arithmetic that looks right and describes something the algorithm never computes.
questions.hint: Square each coordinate difference, add the pair of squares, and keep the smaller total.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The update step in k-means
questions.learningObjective: compute an updated centroid as the mean of its members
questions.stem: A group holds the three points (1,2), (3,2) and (2,8). The update step replaces the group's centre with the mean of its members. What is the y-coordinate of the new centre?
questions.explanation: The y-coordinate is (2 + 2 + 8) divided by 3, which is 4, and the x-coordinate is likewise (1 + 3 + 2) divided by 3, which is 2, so the new centre is (2,4). Reporting 2 for the y-coordinate means the x-coordinate has been read off instead, and dividing by 2 rather than by 3 gives 6. The step itself is worth pausing on: the centre is a summary of the points that were just assigned, so the third point at y=8 is what drags the centre upward, and a group that had lost that point to a competitor would see its centre fall back to 2 on the following pass.
questions.hint: Add the three y-values and divide by the number of members, not by the number of coordinates.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Within-group sum of squared distances
questions.learningObjective: compute the within-group sum of squared distances
questions.stem: Six points on a line are grouped as {1, 2, 3} and {10, 12}. What is the total within-group sum of squared distances of the points from their own group means?
questions.explanation: The first group has mean 2, so its squared deviations are 1, 0 and 1, giving 2, and the second has mean 11, so its squared deviations are 1 and 1, giving 2; the two add to 4. A figure of 2 comes from computing only one group, and 21 is what you get by measuring both groups from the single mean of all six points, which is the k=1 objective rather than the k=2 one. The identity that makes this quick is that the sum of squared deviations from a mean equals the sum of the squares minus the count times the square of the mean, and the cross-check of 4 is also the objective value the first assignment step would report for this grouping.
questions.hint: Take each group's own mean, square the deviations inside it, and add the two totals.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A starting centre placed on an extreme value
questions.learningObjective: predict what an extreme value does when it is chosen as a starting centre
questions.stem: One row records 9,400 in a column where the other 499 rows all sit between 10 and 60, and a k=2 run seeds its two centres by picking rows at random. What does that one row do to the run?

options.text: If it lands as a starting centre it can gather a group of one, leaving the real structure a single undivided clump
Nothing, because a single row cannot move a centre that is the mean of hundreds of rows
options.misconception: believes one row is powerless against a mean over many rows

options.text: It drags both centres towards it, so the two groups end up closer together than the data warrants
options.misconception: imagines one extreme value pulling both centres rather than forming its own

options.text: It is discarded automatically, since distance-based methods drop values far from every centre
options.misconception: believes clustering methods remove extreme values on their own

questions.explanation: The assignment step is a competition, so if the extreme row starts as a centre it wins every point near it, and since nothing else is anywhere near 9,400 it can finish with a group containing only itself while the remaining 499 rows are squeezed into the other group. The distance from that lone point to the nearest other point is enormous, which is exactly what makes the first arrangement's objective worse than the second, and the second arrangement is the one that recovers the structure. The general point is that seeding is the one part of the algorithm with no defence built in, which is why starting centres are drawn with a rule that keeps seeds apart and, better, away from extreme rows.
questions.hint: Ask which points the extreme row is nearer to than any other point is to each other.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Two columns on incompatible scales
questions.learningObjective: explain how column scale distorts a distance-based grouping
questions.stem: Two columns describe the same customers: height near 170 centimetres with a spread of 8, and annual spend near 4000 currency units with a spread of 1500. A distance-based clustering reads both columns. What is wrong, and what addresses it?

options.text: Spend dominates every distance, so the grouping is really a grouping by spend; a correlation distance ignores scale
Both columns contribute equally, because a distance weighs every column the same whatever its units
options.misconception: believes column units cannot affect a Euclidean distance

options.text: Height is discarded as noise, since a column with the smaller spread carries no information
options.misconception: reads a small spread as evidence that a column is useless

options.text: Spend is converted into centimetres, which cannot be done because the two units are different
options.misconception: believes the fix is a conversion between the two units

questions.explanation: A squared Euclidean distance adds the squared differences from the two columns, so a column with a spread two hundred times larger contributes roughly forty thousand times as much to almost every comparison, and the grouping ends up being a threshold on spend with height along for the ride. A distance that normalises each column first, such as the correlation between the two standardised rows, ignores scale and units entirely and compares customers by shape rather than by size. The uncomfortable corollary is that a scale-sensitive metric is not automatically wrong: if spend is genuinely the thing you care about, then letting it dominate is a decision rather than a defect.
questions.hint: Ask which column's squared differences are larger, and by roughly how much.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Two runs, raw columns and standardised columns
questions.learningObjective: read what a change between two runs of a clustering establishes
questions.stem: A clustering is run twice on identical rows. The first run uses raw columns and returns two groups split almost entirely by the currency column. The second standardises every column to mean zero and unit standard deviation and returns groups that also separate on the size column. What has the second run shown?

options.text: The raw grouping was tracking the scale of the currency column rather than anything the data says about customers
The raw grouping was the correct one, since rescaling should not change which rows sit near each other
options.misconception: assumes rescaling is scale-free in its effect on the grouping

options.text: The data holds no cluster structure, because the two runs disagree about what the groups are
options.misconception: treats disagreement between runs as evidence of no structure

options.text: The size column is the true structure, since a standardised column is by definition the better one
options.misconception: believes standardising a column upgrades it into the real signal

questions.explanation: The currency column's spread is orders of magnitude larger than the others, so a run on raw columns is mostly thresholding that one column and calling it a grouping; standardising puts every column on the same footing and lets the size column contribute, which is why the two runs disagree. The disagreement is therefore information about the metric rather than about the rows, and the useful question becomes which column ought to carry the grouping, which is a decision about the data rather than a fact to be read off a plot. Neither run is automatically right, and treating the second as right by default is the same error as treating the first as right by default.
questions.hint: Ask which column's spread dominates a distance, and what the first run was therefore measuring.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Reading a fall in the objective as k grows
questions.learningObjective: read an objective curve and say what it leaves undetermined
questions.stem: Six values on a line, 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, are clustered. With one group the within-group sum of squared distances is 70; with two groups, {0,2,4} and {6,8,10}, it is 16. By what percentage does the sum fall when the second group is added?
questions.explanation: The sum falls by 70 minus 16, which is 54, and 54 over 70 is 0.7714, so the fall is 77.1 per cent. The 22.9 that remains is the same calculation read as the share of the original variation the two groups fail to explain, and reporting 16 or 70 forgets the baseline entirely. What matters downstream is not the percentage but its shape: one large drop like this, followed by small ones, is the pattern an elbow plot looks for, and it is also the reason a knee chosen from this curve is a judgement rather than a reading, since the objective keeps falling at every k and never reaches zero.
questions.hint: Take the fall of 54 and divide it by the starting value of 70, then convert to a percentage.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: One unit's silhouette value
questions.learningObjective: compute a silhouette value from within and nearest-cluster distances
questions.stem: For one unit, the mean distance to the other units in its own group is 0.40, and the smallest of its mean distances to any other group is 1.00. What is this unit's silhouette value?
questions.explanation: The silhouette is the gap between the distance to the nearest other group and the distance to the own group, divided by the larger of the two, which here is (1.00 - 0.40) over 1.00, or 0.60. Dividing by the smaller of the two instead gives 0.40, and 1 minus the ratio 0.36 is the same answer reached the other way round, which is a useful cross-check because it shows the value is bounded between minus one and one. A negative value would mean the unit sits closer to another group than to its own, and the average of these values across a run is what gets compared when choosing k, which is why one convenient unit cannot carry a decision.
questions.hint: Take the difference between the two distances and divide by the larger of them.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a hierarchical method returns
questions.learningObjective: compare a hierarchical result with a partition method
questions.stem: A hierarchical method is run in place of the partition method on the same rows. What does it hand back that the partition method cannot, and what does that cost?

options.text: A full merge tree showing every level of grouping at once, at the price of committing to one tree
A guaranteed better grouping, because it weighs every possible number of groups at once
options.misconception: believes an exhaustive tree implies an exhaustive search for the best grouping

options.text: A single grouping that needs no choice of k, because the method settles the number itself
options.misconception: believes a method that outputs a tree also outputs the answer from it

options.text: Faster results on large data, because it never repeats the assignment step many times
options.misconception: believes a tree method scales better than repeated reassignment

questions.explanation: The hierarchical method records the height at which every pair of clusters merges, so one run yields a grouping at k equals 2, at k equals 3 and at every other number, and the reader chooses where to read it off rather than paying for a separate run. What it cannot do is revisit a merge: once two clusters have been joined, nothing in the method will later separate them, so a grouping that would have been better is unavailable at any cut. On large data the cost is memory, since the full matrix of pairwise distances has to be held or recomputed, and the honest comparison is against repeated assignment, which is cheap and revisits.
questions.hint: Ask whether an early merge can be undone, and how many groupings one run produces.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What each linkage rule assumes about a merged cluster
questions.learningObjective: state the assumption behind each linkage rule
questions.stem: A set of points is close enough to merge two clusters. One rule would merge them at height 5 and another at height 4. What is each rule assuming about the cluster it is about to build?

options.text: The first takes the farthest pair so the result stays compact, the second the nearest pair so it can chain on
The first takes the nearest pair so the result stays tight, the second the farthest pair so it stays balanced
options.misconception: swaps the two rules and calls chaining a balancing property

options.text: Both assume the result stays compact and differ only in how they count the points in each group
options.misconception: assumes the rules differ in bookkeeping rather than in geometry

options.text: Both assume the two groups are the same size and differ only in the height at which they merge
options.misconception: assumes linkage rules are sensitive to group size

questions.explanation: The rule only has to choose one number to represent the distance between two whole clusters, and the choice is where the assumption lives. Taking the farthest pair means a merge can only happen when no pair is far apart, which keeps the merged cluster compact and tends to produce round groups at the cost of merging later and more sharply. Taking the nearest pair means a merge can happen on one close pair regardless of how far apart the rest are, which is cheap and reveals fine structure but chains distant points together, so a long thin cloud can collapse into one branch. The average rule is the usual compromise, and the reason to care is that a chain is a real grouping artefact rather than a finding.
questions.hint: Ask what each rule would let through: a far pair, or a single close pair.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The second merge under average linkage
questions.learningObjective: compute a merge height under a stated linkage rule
questions.stem: Four points sit at (0,0), (3,0), (0,4) and (3,4). Under average linkage the two closest pairs merge first, and the two resulting groups then merge with each other. At what distance does that second merge happen?
questions.explanation: The four cross distances between the two groups are 4, 5, 5 and 4, and their mean is 18 over 4, which is 4.5. The 4 that the nearest-pair rule would report takes the smallest of those four, and the 5 that the farthest-pair rule reports takes the largest, so the three rules bracket this answer rather than competing with it. Averaging is what stops a single close pair from pulling two otherwise unrelated groups together, at the price of a height that matches no actual pair of points in the data, which is worth remembering when a dendrogram is read as though its merge heights were measurements.
questions.hint: Compute the four distances between the groups, then average them.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: How many groups a dendrogram cut yields
questions.learningObjective: count the groups produced by a cut through a dendrogram
questions.stem: A dendrogram of six units records merge heights of 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.1 and 1.4. A horizontal cut is drawn at height 0.6. How many groups does the cut leave?
questions.explanation: Two merges sit at or below 0.6, those at 0.2 and 0.5, and each merge removes one group from the count, so six units become 6 - 2 = 4 groups. Counting the three merges above the cut gives 3, which is the same number by accident and would be the answer if the cut sat just below 0.8. A cut exactly at a merge height is ambiguous, since the drawing is then a decision about whether the two groups had already become one, so a stated cut is best placed between heights. The counting rule is the same one that makes a tree of n units contain exactly n - 1 merges, which is a useful check that the merge list is complete.
questions.hint: Count the merges at or below the cut and subtract that count from the number of units.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Reading an objective curve across values of k
questions.learningObjective: interpret a curve of the objective across values of k
questions.stem: The within-group sum of squared distances is recorded for k from 1 to 8 as 70, 16, 10, 8.4, 7.9, 7.7, 7.6 and 7.55, and the team plots it looking for the bend. What does the plot show, and what does it leave open?

options.text: One large fall and then small ones, so the bend sits somewhere between 2 and 4 groups and choosing inside that range is a judgement
Four groups is the proven answer, because the values after k equals 4 no longer fall at all
options.misconception: reads a diminishing fall as a value that has stopped falling

options.text: There is no structure, because the sum keeps falling at every value of k that was tried
options.misconception: treats a monotonically falling objective as proof of no structure

options.text: One group is the right answer, because the first step is where the largest single fall occurs
options.misconception: confuses a large fall between two values with a preference for one of them

questions.explanation: The fall from k equals 1 to k equals 2 takes 54 of the 70, and everything after that takes 16 between them and asymptotically approaches zero, so the curve has one clear elbow and a long flat tail. A flat tail is not a plateau: 7.9, 7.7, 7.6 and 7.55 are different numbers, and the objective will keep falling however large k gets, so the curve cannot hand back a unique answer. That is why a knee is read as a region and then settled with something outside the plot, such as whether the groups are usable, and why a curve offered as proof of a particular k is a curve that has been over-read.
questions.hint: Compare the size of each successive fall, and check whether the values ever stop changing.

questions.topic: Comparing silhouette values across values of k
questions.learningObjective: interpret a table of average silhouette values
questions.stem: A table of average silhouette values reads 0.55 at k equals 2, 0.51 at k equals 3, 0.49 at k equals 4 and 0.12 at k equals 5. A report recommends five groups on the grounds that the k equals 5 run separates the rows most cleanly. What is wrong with the recommendation?

options.text: The k equals 5 run peels two rows off and leaves the rest as one clump, which the average reports as a poor fit
Nothing, since the smallest average silhouette belongs to the run that separates the rows best
options.misconception: believes a lower average silhouette means cleaner separation

options.text: The averages cannot be compared across values of k, because the groups do not all have the same size
options.misconception: believes cluster size prevents comparison of average values

options.text: The k equals 2 row is the faulty one, since no real grouping can reach an average of 0.55
options.misconception: dismisses a reported value as impossible without checking it

questions.explanation: The k equals 5 run is the classic two-singleton artefact: two rows far from everything each get a silhouette near 1 because their nearest other group is a long way off, while the remaining rows all sit in one large group and score near 0, and the average of that mixture lands far below the earlier rows. The average is therefore reporting a real property of the grouping, which is that most rows are indistinguishable from each other. A high average is not the same thing as a well separated set of groups, which is why the silhouette is worth reading alongside the sizes of the groups and a picture, rather than on its own.

questions.learningObjective: pair a reading of a cluster centre with a defensible action

options.misconception: reads a high order count as evidence that accounts are dormant

options.misconception: treats a group mean margin as permission to raise prices

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why the same data yields two groupings
questions.learningObjective: explain a non-unique result and what a practitioner changes
questions.stem: Explain why the same clustering run twice on the same data can end in two different groupings, and say what a practitioner changes to reduce how often that happens.

answer.exemplar: The two runs differ because each one starts from centres it picked arbitrarily and then descends, stopping where no single point would gain by moving; a descent has to stop somewhere and nothing tells it where the lowest stopping point is, so two starting points can reach two different ones. The practitioner does not try to remove the arbitrariness, only to stop it deciding the answer: draw several sets of starting centres, run each one, and keep the run that ends with the lowest objective value, which turns one arbitrary pick into a small sample of the possibilities. That is a reduction in how often a poor start wins, not a proof that the winner is best, and the sentence that overstates it is the one claiming the best grouping has now been found, because no restart can establish that. Where a result has to be reproducible for an audit, the deeper fix is to fix the starting rule and record it, so that the same data and the same seed give the same groups rather than a group that has to be explained after the fact.

questions.explanation: The result is non-unique because the algorithm commits to starting centres before it knows anything about the data, and every later step is a descent that can only find a stopping point rather than the best one. Restarts fix the practical symptom because a poor start shows up as a worse final objective value, so keeping the best of several runs is a cheap improvement with nothing else required. What restarts cannot deliver is certainty, and the sentence to distrust is the one that reports the winning run as the correct grouping, since a genuinely better starting point nobody tried would have produced a better value.
questions.hint: Ask what the algorithm decided before it had seen the data, and what can be sampled rather than solved.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The steps of a k-means run
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of a k-means run from scaling to convergence
questions.stem: Put the stages of a k-means run in the order that produces a result which can be trusted rather than merely produced.

options.text: Rescale the columns so no single unit of measurement dominates the distances between rows
Choose starting centres, more than one set of them, so the run is not settled by one arbitrary pick
Assign every point to its nearest centre, which is the only step that can lower the objective outright
Recompute each centre from the points just assigned to it and repeat until the assignments stop moving

questions.explanation: Rescaling comes first because every later distance depends on it, and starting centres come before the first assignment because that is the only decision in the run made without looking at the points. Assignment and updating then alternate, each one improving the objective for the other to follow, and the run ends when an assignment changes nothing, which is the first moment at which the grouping and the centres agree with each other. Stopping earlier, or stopping after a fixed number of passes for convenience, is how a run reports a grouping that its own centres do not support, and the last stage is also the one that decides when the answer is final.
questions.hint: Ask which steps are decisions about the data and which are a repeated pair of operations.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Distances crowding together in many dimensions
questions.learningObjective: explain why nearest neighbours stop being informative in many dimensions
questions.stem: A similarity search across 900 columns returns every item as roughly equally far from every other, so the returned nearest neighbours are close to arbitrary. What has gone wrong?

options.text: In many dimensions the distances crowd together, so a gap of a few per cent carries almost no information
The columns must be missing values, since complete data is what makes the distances crowd
options.misconception: blames missing data for a geometric effect of dimensionality

options.text: The table must be too small, since crowding only happens when there are fewer rows than columns
options.misconception: believes the row count relative to the columns is what matters

options.text: Nothing is wrong, so the arbitrary ranking is evidence that the data holds no structure
options.misconception: reads the crowding effect as evidence that no structure exists

questions.topic: The loading of a variable on the first component

options.misconception: says interpretation has to be imposed rather than read off

options.misconception: assumes rescaling only flips signs

questions.topic: What a factor is in a factor model

The first alone carries 36 over 50, or 0.72, and the second alone 0.18, so the two together are neither of those and adding 0.72 and 0.18 is the right way to see where the figure came from. questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Explained variance is a statement about spread
questions.learningObjective: explain what an explained-variance ratio does not establish
questions.stem: Explain why a high explained-variance ratio on the first component is not by itself a reason to keep only that component, and give the sentence that overstates it.

answer.exemplar: The ratio measures how much of the spread in the columns a component captures, and spread is not the same thing as signal: a column can vary enormously because of a recording artefact, a season, or a quantity that happens to be measured on a large scale, and none of those help a prediction. What a downstream use needs is whatever it is trying to use, so the count of components has to be argued from the task, not from the curve. The sentence that overstates it says that since the first component explains most of the variance, most of the information is in the first component, and the slip in it is the substitution of spread for information, which is what makes a component that carries 3 per cent look disposable when it may be the one that carries the part a classifier depends on. A safer rule of thumb is to keep every component that the downstream step is measurably helped or hurt by, and to record that comparison, because it is evidence about the use rather than about the data.

questions.explanation: The ratio is a statement about geometry and usefulness is a statement about a task, and the two come apart in both directions: a leading component can carry most of the spread and none of what matters, and a later one can carry a few per cent and be the difference between working and not. The overstating sentence is the one that treats a variance share as though it were a share of the information, which no calculation supports. questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a flat map of high-dimensional data can show
questions.learningObjective: explain the limits of a two-dimensional embedding as cluster evidence
questions.stem: Explain why a flat picture of high-dimensional data is weak evidence about how many groups exist, and give the failure a reader should look for.

answer.exemplar: The picture is a projection, and a projection can move points that were far apart into a crowded neighbourhood while pushing apart points that were close, so apparent clumps and gaps in the plane are statements about the projection as much as about the data. A two-dimensional map of a space with hundreds of columns has room for perhaps a handful of well-separated blobs, and the eye supplies the rest: neighbours that sit side by side read as members of a group, and a thin gap between two blobs reads as a boundary that is not there in the original columns. The failure a reader should look for is a group whose apparent tightness comes entirely from the projection, which shows up as a group that dissolves when a different number of axes or a different neighbour setting is used, and the practical defence is to require a group to reappear under a change the picture itself did not choose. Counting blobs on a map is otherwise a way of reading the method's output as if it were the data, which is the mistake the method was built to make possible.

questions.explanation: A picture is a compression, and the compression is lossy in ways that are not visible in the picture, so a clump is a hypothesis about a neighbourhood rather than a measurement of one. The specific failure to look for is a group that is an artefact of the settings used to make the map, which is why the same data redrawn with different settings should reproduce any group worth acting on. Treating the eye's segmentation of a busy plane as a count of groups is the most common way a map gets over-read, and it is cheap to avoid by asking what would have to be true of the original columns for the group to be real.
questions.hint: Ask what the picture leaves out, and what a group would look like if the picture were the reason for it.

options.text: It avoids centring, since centring is unnecessary once the factors have been extracted
options.misconception: claims a step of the method can be skipped

options.text: It works for any matrix, whereas a covariance decomposition only applies to a square symmetric one
options.misconception: overstates what a decomposition can accept

questions.explanation: On a centred matrix the singular values turn out to be the square roots of the covariance eigenvalues and the left factors are the same directions as the covariance eigenvectors, so the one computation delivers both the scores and the variance carried by each direction, which is why the method is usually carried out this way. The saving is real, since a covariance matrix never has to be formed and the factor loadings fall out directly, and it is also why a decomposition of an uncentred matrix looks so different: there the largest factor absorbs the mean. The uniqueness claim is wrong in the useful sense, since eigenvectors are only determined up to sign and any rotation among near-equal eigenvalues is equally valid.
questions.hint: Ask what the singular values of a centred matrix turn out to be.

questions.topic: The neighbour setting in a UMAP
questions.learningObjective: identify which parameter of a UMAP changes the layout and how
questions.stem: A UMAP is fitted with a setting for how many nearby records each record is matched to, and a second run uses a much smaller value. What is the expected effect on the two layouts?

options.misconception: assumes a parameter has no effect on the output

options.misconception: assumes fewer neighbours enlarges the groups it draws

questions.stem: Six records form two groups of three, {0, 1000}, {10, 1020}, {5, 1010} and {0, 2000}, {10, 2020}, {5, 2010}. The first column is a dose in milligrams and the second is a cost in hundreds of currency units. Used as recorded, what share of the within-group sum of squared distances comes from the cost column?

Standardising each column first divides out the spread and makes the two shares equal at a half each, and that is the whole point of the comparison: the grouping was being decided mostly by whichever column happened to be recorded in large numbers. A distance that normalises each column answers a different question from one that lets magnitudes count, and which question is wanted is a decision about the data.
questions.hint: Compute each column's squared deviations inside the groups, total them, and take the cost column's share.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Averaging the silhouettes inside one group
questions.learningObjective: compute a group's mean silhouette from raw distances
questions.stem: Two units in the same group have a mean distance to their own group of 0.40 and 0.60, and a nearest-other-group mean distance of 0.80 and 0.75. What is this group's mean silhouette?
questions.explanation: The first unit's silhouette is (0.80 - 0.40) over 0.80, which is 0.5, and the second is (0.75 - 0.60) over 0.75, which is 0.2, so the group mean is 0.35. The 0.7 that looks tempting is the sum of the two silhouettes rather than their average, and the 0.3 is what you get by averaging the two raw distances instead of the two ratios, which is a different quantity and does not mean the same thing. Averaging the ratios rather than the parts is what keeps the measure comparable across groups of different tightness, since a group whose distances are all large should not be penalised simply for being far from the origin of the measurement.
questions.hint: Turn each unit's two distances into a silhouette, then average the two silhouettes.

questions.topic: Averaging the silhouette over all records
questions.learningObjective: weight group means by group size when averaging
questions.stem: A run produced two groups: one of three records with a mean silhouette of 0.6, and one of two records with a mean silhouette of minus 0.2. What is the average silhouette over all five records?

The 0.2 that comes from averaging the two group means equally is the mistake, and it is a consequential one because a two-record group and a three-record group are being given the same say. questions.topic: A covariance between two columns
questions.learningObjective: compute a sample covariance from raw values
questions.stem: For four records a column takes the values 1, 2, 3 and 4, and another takes 1, 3, 6 and 10. What is their sample covariance, using the divisor n minus one?
questions.explanation: The first column's deviations from its mean of 2.5 are -1.5, -0.5, 0.5 and 1.5, the second's from its mean of 5 are -4, -2, 1 and 5, and the products are 6, 1, 0.5 and 7.5, summing to 15, which over 3 is 5. The route through the raw products agrees: the column products sum to 1, 6, 18 and 40, so 65 over 4 gives 16.25, and 16.25 minus 2.5 times 5 leaves the same 5. The 3.75 that appears from dividing by 4 is the population covariance, a different convention rather than a wrong answer, and it matters here because a covariance divided by n and one divided by n minus one are both in circulation and mixing them with a standard deviation from the other convention silently rescales a correlation.
questions.hint: Multiply matched deviations from the two means, add the products, and divide by one less than the number of records.

questions.topic: A correlation from a covariance and two spreads
questions.learningObjective: recover a correlation from a covariance and two standard deviations
questions.stem: Two columns over the same four records take the values 1, 2, 3 and 4 and 1, 3, 6 and 10, and their sample covariance is 5. What is the correlation between the two columns, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: The first column has a sample variance of 5 over 3, so a spread of 1.29, and the second has 46 over 3, so a spread of 3.92; dividing the covariance of 5 by the product of the two gives 0.99, and the same value comes from dividing the sum of the products, 15, by the square root of the two sums of squared deviations, 5 and 46. Two routes agreeing on something just short of 1 is the check worth making, since a correlation of exactly 1 requires the points to lie on a straight line and four scattered points never quite do. The trap in this calculation is a covariance carried over from a population convention and a spread from a sample one, which inflates the result beyond 1 and is a useful signal that the two divisors have been mixed.
questions.hint: Divide the covariance by the product of the two standard deviations.

questions.stem: One column takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 across five records and a second column takes 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50. What is the standardised distance between the first record and the last?

The shortcut is that the second column is an exact multiple of the first, so after standardising the two coordinates are identical for every record and the distance is just the gap on one column times the square root of two. questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The variance a component's scores carry
questions.learningObjective: read a component's variance from the eigenvalues
questions.stem: A four-column decomposition has eigenvalues 5, 3, 1.5 and 0.5, and a total variance of 10. What is the variance of the scores produced by the second component?
questions.explanation: The scores produced by a component have a variance equal to that component's eigenvalue, so the second carries 3 of the 10, and the check is that 10 minus 5, minus 1.5 and minus 0.5 leaves 3. The 0.3 is the same figure divided by the total, which is the share rather than the variance, and 10 is the total, which belongs to no single component. The reason the variance of the scores equals the eigenvalue is that the components are orthonormal, so their scores are uncorrelated and the spread of the data is simply divided among them without being counted twice.

questions.topic: Two columns that are the same column
questions.learningObjective: explain the ceiling a duplicated feature puts on one component
questions.stem: A four-column correlation matrix has one column an exact copy of a second, and the remaining two columns are uncorrelated with everything. What is the largest share of the total variance any single component can carry?
questions.explanation: The duplicated pair forms a block whose total variance is 2, and the block's spread splits between one direction where the two columns rise together and one where they oppose, so no single component can hold more than the block's 2, and the two remaining columns contribute 1 each, giving a total of 4 and a ceiling of a half. The 1.0 is the belief that one component can absorb everything, which is exactly what a duplicated feature seems to promise, and the 0.25 is the ceiling if the duplication were spread across four columns instead. The matrix is trustworthy, since a symmetric matrix cannot be the product of a faulty computation
options.misconception: infers correctness from a structural property of any valid result

options.misconception: confuses symmetry with the absence of off-diagonal values

options.text: The matrix needs no further checks, since a negative entry proves the data are nonlinear
options.misconception: reads one negative entry as a statement about functional form

options.misconception: treats every visible feature as a segment worth acting on

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a silhouette cannot settle
questions.learningObjective: explain the limits of a silhouette value as a criterion
questions.stem: Explain why an average silhouette value is not enough on its own to choose a grouping, and give the failure it cannot see.

answer.exemplar: The silhouette compares a record's distance to its own group with its distance to the nearest other group, which says whether each record is on the correct side of a boundary, and that is a weaker claim than saying the groups exist. It cannot see shapes: a long thin group wrapped around another, or two crescents that are well separated from everything but nowhere near each other, both score badly however real they are, and a method that improves the average by making the groups round will be preferred. It cannot see sizes either, since a run that peels two records off scores far worse than one that does not, which is a feature rather than a bug but does mean the measure is biased against small groups. The failure to watch for is therefore a grouping that is genuinely present and non-convex, which the average will penalise for every additional group that reveals it, and the defence is to read the silhouettes alongside the picture and the group sizes rather than ranking runs by the average alone.

questions.explanation: The measure is a statement about boundary placement, and using it as a statement about structure imports an assumption it does not license, namely that good groups are compact and roughly round. It also carries a built-in preference against small groups, since a peeled-off record scores poorly against the large group it left, so a ranking by average is a ranking under two assumptions rather than one. What it does give, cheaply and honestly, is a way to notice runs that place records badly, and that is a real service even when it cannot rank the rest.
questions.hint: Ask what shape the measure assumes, and what it does to a group that is small or not round.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a component is not a factor
questions.learningObjective: explain what a decomposition does not claim that a factor model does
questions.stem: Explain what a principal component does not claim that a factor model does, and give the sentence that treats the two as interchangeable.

answer.exemplar: A principal component is the direction in which the data are widest, and nothing in its construction says that anything generated the variables; a factor model says the variables are measurements of a smaller number of things that cannot be observed, and that is a claim about the world which can be wrong in ways the numbers cannot check. Three practical consequences follow. A decomposition is free to produce as many components as there are columns and every one of them has a direction whether or not it means anything, whereas a factor model fixes the count in advance and has to justify it. A component's scores are a rescaling of the data and reproducing the data exactly, so there is no question of a residual, while a factor model has residuals that are supposed to be noise. And two factors with similar patterns can be given different names and different rotations, which is a symptom of a model that is not pinned down by the data. The sentence that treats them as interchangeable says the components were interpreted as factors, which quietly converts a description of spread into a claim about a mechanism that nothing in the decomposition supports.

questions.explanation: The difference is one of claim, not of arithmetic: both are linear and both produce loadings, but only one of them asserts an underlying quantity and therefore takes on the risk of being wrong about it. Reading a component as a factor is not a harmless habit of speech, because a factor with a name invites a mechanism to be designed around it while a component does not. If a mechanism is what the study needs, a model that states one and reports its residuals is the tool for the job, and if it is not, the simpler description was already sufficient.
questions.hint: Ask whether the component is claimed to generate the variables or only to summarise them.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Choosing a method for a nested structure
questions.learningObjective: explain when a merge tree is the better tool
questions.stem: Explain when a merge tree is a better tool than repeated assignment, and give the symptom that should prompt the choice.

answer.exemplar: A merge tree is the better tool when the structure is nested, because a tree shows every level of grouping at once and the level you want is a place to cut rather than a run to repeat, and it is the only way to see a small tight subgroup sitting inside a large diffuse one without losing the outer structure. Repeated assignment is the better tool when the number of groups is known, when the data is large enough that a full matrix of pairwise distances is out of reach, or when a group has been split wrongly and would have to be merged back. The symptom that should prompt the switch is a run that keeps producing a few large groups plus a spray of tiny ones, since that pattern usually means groups exist at several scales and a single partition is the wrong shape for the answer. The cost of the tree is that it commits: once two branches have merged they cannot be separated, so a tree built on a metric that does not suit the data is a tree that has locked in the wrong answer, and a tree is also expensive on large tables, which is why the two are often run together and the tree is used to explain a partition rather than to produce one.

questions.explanation: The choice follows from the shape of the answer wanted, since a tree is a whole hierarchy and a partition is one level of it, so asking which question is being asked settles which tool applies. The practical argument for the tree is diagnostic: it shows at which distance structure appears and disappears, which is information a single run throws away. The argument against is irreversibility, since no cut of a wrong tree recovers a grouping that was lost at an early merge, and that is why a metric worth trusting matters more for a tree than for repeated assignment.
questions.hint: Ask whether the answer is one level of grouping or the whole hierarchy, and what a wrong merge costs.

Choose the distance between records and the rule for the distance between two groups
Merge the closest pair or groups and record the height at which they joined

questions.explanation: Rescaling and the two metric choices come first because a merge height is a distance, so it inherits every problem in the units and every property of the rule that turns a set of pairwise distances into one number for two groups. The merging itself is then mechanical, and what makes the record worth keeping is the height at each join, since that is the only place the judgement about the rule is visible afterwards. Cutting comes last and is a separate decision, which is worth keeping separate from the construction because a tree built on a metric nobody chose deliberately will still produce a plausible-looking figure at whatever height is cut.
questions.hint: Ask which choices the recorded heights depend on, and when the cut decision is made.
